“Philemon — Faith Works”: The episode reads Paul's short letter about Onesimus, an enslaved man who ran away, against Roman ideas of citizenship, slavery and patronage. It also points to Paul's playful but pointed tone and his hope that Philemon will welcome Onesimus out of conviction rather than fear of consequences.

Says Paul writes as Christ's prisoner, not as an apostle with rank, and as a friend to Philemon, then adds Apphia, Archippus and the church that met in the house. Guzik takes the house church as an ordinary early pattern and finds the greeting unusually personal for a letter that also reached a congregation.

"Unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellow-laborer." If "beloved," then his confidence is not boldness nor forwardness, but a proof of much affection. If a "fellow-laborer," then not only may he be instructed in such a matter, but he ought to acknowledge it as a favor. For he is gratifying himself, he is building up the same work. So that apart from any request, he says, thou hast another necessity for granting the favor.

"And to the Church in thy house." Here he has not omitted even the slaves. For he knew that often even the words of slaves have power to overthrow their master; and more especially when his request was in behalf of a slave. And perhaps it was they particularly who exasperated him. He does not suffer them therefore to fall into envy, having honored them by including them in a salutation with their masters. And neither does he allow the master to take offense.

"Grace to you, and peace." By mentioning "grace," he brings his own sins to his remembrance. Consider, he says, how great things God has pardoned in thee, how by grace thou art saved. Imitate thy Lord. And he prays for "peace" to him; and naturally: for it comes then when we imitate Him, then grace abides. Since even that servant who was unmerciful to his fellow-servants, until he demanded the hundred pence, had the grace of his master abiding on him.

He does not immediately at the commencement ask the favor, but having first admired the man, and having praised him for his good actions, and having shown no small proof of his love, that he always made mention of him in his prayers, and having said that many are refreshed by him, and that he is obedient and complying in all things; then he puts it last of all, by this particularly putting him to the blush. For if others obtain the things which they ask, much more Paul.

Barclay finds it remarkable that Paul asks a favor at all, and notes that he drops the title of apostle to write as a prisoner and friend, appealing to love alone. He pictures Philemon's house as a place where God's people were rested, and prefers the reading of verse 6 as generous sharing that leads to deeper knowledge of Christ.

"Hearing," he says, "of thy love." This is wonderful, and much greater than if being present he had seen it when he was present. For it is plain that from its being excessive it had become manifest, and had reached even to Paul. And yet the distance between Rome and Phrygia was not small. For he seems to have been there from the mention of Archippus.
6: Reads the opening prayer as Paul's way of praising what is already good in Philemon: his love and faith toward the Lord and the saints. He suggests the sharing of faith in verse 6 may include practical generosity, and that Philemon had already refreshed many believers.

I pray, he says, "that the communication of thy faith may become effectual in the knowledge of every good thing which is in Christ Jesus." Dost thou see him first giving, before he receives, and before he asks a favor himself bestowing a much greater one of his own? "That the communication of thy faith," he says, "may become effectual by the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus"; that is, that thou mayest attain all virtue, that nothing may be deficient.

Wherefore, having much confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what is profitable for love's sake, I rather beseech, since you are such a one, as Paul an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Many praises of Philemon have been set out beforehand. The matter for which he is asked is also such as to be useful both to the one who grants it and to the one who asks. Paul therefore could have commanded rather than requested.

See how great is his prudence, how he confesses the man's faults, and thereby extinguishes his anger. I know, he says, that he was unprofitable. "But now" he will be "profitable to thee and to me." He has not said he will be useful to thee, lest he should contradict it, but he has introduced his own person, that his hopes may seem worthy of credit, "But now," he says, "profitable to thee and to me." For if he was profitable to Paul, who required so great strictness, much more would he be so to his master.

But without your counsel I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as it were of necessity, but voluntary. The question asked by very many, and very often taken up again, is why God, in making man, did not create him good and upright. It can be resolved from the present passage. Reads Paul's cautious words, "perhaps," as a hint that God used the separation for good, so that Philemon receives Onesimus back for good as a brother. Guzik argues that calling a slave a brother undermines slavery from within, because changed hearts do more than laws.

That you might receive him eternal. No one is the eternal master of his slave: for his power, and the condition of each of them, is ended by death. But Onesimus, who was made eternal through the faith of Christ, having received the spirit of liberty, began, from a slave, to be no longer a slave but a brother to Philemon, who is eternal because he too had believed in Christ: a dearest brother, an eternal brother; also to the eternal Apostle himself and to his master, to whom, as the condition of the flesh joined…

If therefore you have me as a partner, receive him as me. Philemon desired to have Paul as a partner, and, believing in Christ, he certainly wished to make such progress as to become like Paul and to share with him in his chains. Let us consider, therefore, how greatly Onesimus is praised here, and how far he is said to have progressed: for he is to be received as the Apostle is, and his master ought to desire his companionship just as he desires Paul's.

"Put that to mine account," he says, that is, reckon the debt to me, "I will repay it." Then also with that spiritual pleasantry, "I Paul write it with mine own hand." At once movingly and pleasantly; if when Paul did not refuse to execute a bond for him, he should refuse to receive him! This would both shame Philemon into compliance, and bring Onesimus out of trouble. "I write it," he says, "with mine own hand." Nothing is more affectionate than these "bowels," nothing more earnest, nothing more zealous.

"Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow-workers." Why then does he put Luke last? And yet he elsewhere says, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Tim. iv. 11), and "Demas," he says, was one of those who "forsook him, having loved the present world." (2 Tim. iv. 10.) All these things, although they are mentioned elsewhere, yet nevertheless ought not to be passed over here without enquiry, nor ought we merely to hear them as things of course. But how comes he to say that he who forsook him salutes them?

Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Just as the people of Israel is numbered by the better part of man, the head, as Scripture says, according to their heads (Num. 1:2), so the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is indeed in the whole man and in every part of the saints. But by synecdoche it is said of the whole man, from the greater and better part, that is, the spirit: Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
